topics.title: 52.1 Thread-per-connection
topics.summary: A thread-per-connection design assigns a worker to each accepted client. Blocking I/O becomes straightforward because one slow connection blocks its own worker rather than the entire server loop. The control flow resembles a sequential protocol handler. The cost grows with active connections: thread stacks, scheduler state, per-connection buffers, and synchronization overhead accumulate. An unbounded thread-per-connection loop can exhaust resources before useful work completes. Bound admission and ensure every thread is joined or otherwise owned through shutdown.

topics.title: 52.2 Connection state
topics.summary: Connection state includes protocol progress, input and output buffers, authentication or session information, deadlines, and lifecycle status. A connection may be reading a prefix, reading a body, computing a response, writing a partial response, or closing. Make state transitions explicit. “Socket exists” is not enough to determine which operation is valid next. A half-closed connection can still have data to drain or a response to send, depending on the protocol. Cleanup should occur only when no worker or event handler can still reference the connection object.

topics.title: 52.3 Shared resources
topics.summary: Connections compete for descriptors, memory, CPU, downstream services, caches, and application data. Per-connection limits do not replace global limits. A thousand individually acceptable requests can collectively overwhelm a shared database or work queue. Define budgets at each stage. An accepted socket may count against a connection limit, a parsed request against a queued-work limit, and an executing task against a worker limit. Transfer the corresponding ownership credits when work moves between stages, and release them on every failure path.

topics.title: 52.4 Synchronization
topics.summary: Shared application state requires the same synchronization rules developed in Parts X and XI. A server should avoid holding global locks while waiting for a client or downstream service. Slow external activity inside a critical section can stall otherwise independent clients. Use snapshots, immutable request objects, and bounded queues to separate I/O from protected updates. A worker pool limits simultaneously executing handlers, but an unbounded queue in front of it can still consume unlimited memory and produce extreme waiting times.

topics.title: 52.5 Resource exhaustion
topics.summary: Exhaustion occurs when demand exceeds a resource limit. Symptoms include failed thread creation, descriptor exhaustion, allocation failure, long queues, and timeout cascades. Rejecting or deferring work deliberately is often safer than accepting everything and failing unpredictably later. A robust policy specifies admission limits, maximum frame sizes, idle and whole-request deadlines, output-buffer limits, and shutdown behavior. Per-operation socket timeouts alone do not defeat a client that makes tiny amounts of progress just before each timeout; a whole-request deadline bounds the complete transaction.

topics.title: Worked example — Derive an admission budget
topics.summary: Assume a hypothetical service budget , not a measurement of the host system: The descriptor bound is 1024 - 64 = 960 clients when each client uses one descriptor. The modeled per-client memory is 72 KiB. The remaining memory is 96 MiB, which permits floor(96 × 1024 / 72) = 1365 clients under those assumptions. The combined arithmetic ceiling is therefore 960. Choosing an operational cap of 256 leaves headroom. Its modeled client memory is 256 × 72 KiB = 18 MiB ; adding the 32-MiB base gives 50 MiB. This does not include every possible kernel buffer or thread reservation. The assumptions must be replaced with measurements and explicit accounting before using the number as a deployment limit. topics.title: Exercise 4: Choose a design
topics.summary: Would switching to an event loop remove the need for limits? Compare the selected design with this plausible alternative: A worker pool caps active work; a bounded queue and admission policy are still needed to control waiting work.

blocks.title: Hint — open after your first attempt
blocks.text: Name the expected change or workload first. Compare guarantees, ownership, and the cost of added machinery.

blocks.title: Explained answer — compare your reasoning
blocks.text: No. It may reduce thread stacks, but connections, input buffers, queued output, timeouts, and application work still consume bounded resources. The extended lab uses this reasoning: Checking the count and incrementing it form one critical section, otherwise two arrivals could both observe spare capacity. The gate bounds admitted work, not every byte the server owns. Callers must still pair successful admission with release on every completion and error path; a scope-based permit object is a useful next extension. Another solution is reasonable if it meets the same contract with fewer moving parts for its actual workload.

LECTURE NARRATION
A concurrent server handles overlapping client lifecycles while sharing finite resources. The architecture must balance simplicity, throughput, latency, isolation, and failure containment. The most important scaling question is not “How many threads can I create?” but “What resources does one admitted connection consume, and what happens when the budget is exhausted?”
